A modern out-of-order superscalar CPU is not a simple “fetch → execute → write-back” machine. It is a large speculative, dynamically scheduled, register-renamed, memory-ordering-aware pipeline whose goal is to keep many independent instructions in flight while preserving the illusion of sequential, architecturally correct execution.

Below is a detailed technical walkthrough of the major stages and mechanisms.

---

## 1. High-Level Pipeline Overview

A simplified modern x86/ARM-style out-of-order core looks like this:

```text
Branch predictor
       |
       v
Fetch -> Decode -> Rename -> Dispatch -> Issue -> Execute -> Memory -> Retire
       |          |         |          |        |         |        |
       +----------+---------+----------+--------+---------+--------+
                    ROB / scheduler / physical registers / queues
```

The key architectural idea is:

- **In-order front end**: fetch and decode usually proceed in program order.
- **Out-of-order back end**: execution happens as soon as operands are ready.
- **In-order retirement**: instructions commit in program order to preserve
